title: Love your enemies (Luke 6:27–38)
hookLine: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over

lines: A MEASURING BASKET AT A STALL.
cards: A grain seller dips a measuring basket. A stingy seller scoops loosely, so there's air in it.
A generous one fills it, presses it down with his hands, gives it a shake so the grain settles, and fills it again until it heaps and spills over the rim. Then he pours it into the fold of your robe.
You walk away with more than you paid for. Jesus ends a hard teaching with that picture.

teach.h: LOVE HERE IS ACTION, NOT FEELING.
teach.b: The sermon on the plain keeps going, and it gets harder. "But I say to you that hear: Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you." Then, one after another: bless those who curse you.
Pray for those who mistreat you. If someone strikes you on one cheek, offer the other. Give to everyone who asks.
Do to others as you'd have them do to you. Love here is not a feeling. Every item is an action: do good, bless, pray, give.
Jesus doesn't ask you to like your enemy. He asks you to act for their good.

teach.h: BE MERCIFUL, AS YOUR FATHER IS.
teach.b: Then the reason: be merciful, as your Father also is merciful; God, he says, is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.
And then the picture from the market: "Give, and it shall be given to you: good measure and pressed down and shaken together and running over shall they give into your bosom."
With the same measure you use, it will be measured back to you. That's not a business deal.
It's about the size of the basket you carry.
Luke also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, and he shows it happening: Stephen, dying under the stones, prays for the people throwing them.
The command is hard, and Luke doesn't soften it. But it never says an enemy stops being dangerous. Loving an enemy can mean keeping a safe distance and still praying for them.

how: Catholics pray for enemies in personal prayer and in the prayers of the faithful at Mass; forgiving offenses and praying for the living and the dead are among the Church's spiritual works of mercy.

o: love that acts for another's good
a warm feeling of fondness for friends

games.q: love your enemies — tap the pairs.
p: as your Father also is merciful

s: in Luke, loving an enemy means feeling warmly toward them
every command is an action: do good, bless, pray, give.
the running-over measure is poured into the fold of a robe
Luke 6:38 says into your bosom: the fold of the garment.
Luke also wrote Acts, where Stephen prays for those stoning him
Acts 7:60: Stephen asks the Lord not to lay this sin to their charge.

games.q: someone who has wronged you asks you for a favor today. by Luke 6, what's the move?
o: do it, and give a little more than they asked.
do it, but make sure they know you're keeping score.
games.why: Luke 6 says give to everyone who asks, and give good measure. the measure you use is the measure you'll get back.

practice: Let one person come to mind who has hurt you or works against you; it doesn't have to be the worst one, start small. Say their name inside once, and notice what happens in your chest.
If you pray, ask God for one good thing for them, health, peace, a better day than they gave you; if you don't, simply wish it for them, because you don't have to feel warm to do it.

wordCard.voice: agape. Greek for love that acts for another's good: in Luke, this love is something you do, bless, pray, give, with a generous measure. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: love your enemies. The verb is agapao, kin to agape, love that acts for another's good.
